Gold also remains sensitive to developments in oil and refined fuel markets, where the recent sharp price declines have raised hopes that inflationary pressures may soon ease. If sustained, lower energy costs could feed through to broader inflation measures in the coming months, potentially challenging the market’s increasingly hawkish Fed outlook. For now, however, gold remains caught between the immediate headwind from rising yields and a potential longer-term benefit from easing inflation expectations and a less aggressive Fed tightening cycle.

Container freight rates ease as demand slows and shipping disruptions fade

Global container freight rates declined for a third consecutive week, with the Drewry World Container Index falling to USD 4,305 per 40-foot container. The benchmark remains within the narrow USD 400 trading range established in July, but this apparent stability masks significant divergence between major shipping routes.

Trans-Pacific rates have been particularly strong, with Shanghai-to-New York and Los Angeles rates reaching four-year highs last month before easing. The surge reflected robust US import demand, pre-holiday inventory building, elevated fuel costs and Middle East shipping disruptions. Maersk also recently highlighted growing demand for shipping services linked to the global rollout of AI infrastructure. By contrast, Shanghai-to-Europe rates have declined steadily since July, supported by improving vessel availability and the gradual restoration of shorter routes through the Red Sea and Suez Canal.

The latest broad-based decline reflects seasonal demand weakness, easing congestion, lower fuel costs and improving vessel availability as shorter routes release additional capacity. Despite remaining around 85% above its 2023–25 average, the Drewry Index faces further downside pressure unless fresh supply-chain disruptions emerge, particularly on the previously overheated Trans-Pacific routes.

Oil down, but energy markets remain far from normal. Brent has slumped 18% this month as Middle East supply recovers, yet diesel and LNG remain tight.
